<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 23 Oct 2026 11:03:11 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[PTSB says Axis bid interest ‘highly speculative’ as it sticks to Bawag deal timeline]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/ptsb-says-axis-bid-interest-highly-speculative-as-it-sticks-to-bawag-deal-timeline/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/ptsb-says-axis-bid-interest-highly-speculative-as-it-sticks-to-bawag-deal-timeline/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 10:04:12 +0000PTSB said that the 11th-hour bid interest from Axis Capital is “highly speculative and conditional” as the bank confirmed on Friday that a High Court sanctioning hearing on its planned €1.62 billion takeover by Austria’s Bawag will proceed on Tuesday morning as planned.

The 57.5 per cent State-owned bank noted that four shareholders, known to include long-term dissenting investor Scotchstone Capital, led by Piotr Skoczylas, have indicated that they plan to object to the sanction of the deal, being carried out as a so-called scheme of arrangement that requires court approval.

“These shareholders have, over a prolonged period, pursued a number of unsuccessful legal proceedings” since the State effectively nationalised the bank in 2011.

“The court hearing is expected to take place over a number of days. The timing of the judgment, following the satisfaction of scheme conditions and the conclusion of the application for sanction of the scheme, will be a matter for the High Court,” it said.

The statement comes a day after Axis Capital, a corporate advisory firm cofounded by former banker Mark Duffy, said it will ask the High Court next week to delay ratifying PTSB’s takeover by Bawag by up to six weeks as it seeks to put together a potential offer for the bank.

Mark Duffy’s Axis to ask court to delay ratifying Bawag’s PTSB takeover

The company said that investment bank Keefe, Bruyette & Woods (KBW) has introduced it to a “large global investment manager”, which is weighing acting as lead investor in the financing of a potential bid.

“The possible funder is evaluating acting as lead anchor investor in the financing of a possible offer, with the balance of the capital to be syndicated to its limited partners and other co-investors,” Axis said.

KBW has not been engaged by either side. Axis is advised by Berlin-based Quirin Privatbank. Duffy was the chief executive of the now-defunct Bank of Scotland (Ireland), which was closed after the 2008 crash.

“The possible funder has indicated that completing its confirmatory due diligence is essential before it can syndicate the balance of the capital to its partners and provide a formal letter of support,” Axis added.

PTSB confirms in its statement on Friday that no offer has been made by Axis. The bank “is firmly of the view that this latest announcement remains highly speculative and conditional and that no new information has been provided by Axis or its advisers that has changed that position”, it said.

The bank’s board “remains focused on delivering value and certainty to the company’s shareholders and, in accordance with its legal obligations, is continuing to work with Bawag” on completing the planned deal.

Scotchstone also signalled on October 9th that it was considering making an offer for PTSB, but has yet to say whether it has lined up necessary funding.

The chief executive of Bawag said earlier this week that the Austrian banking group was “rising above the noise” as it awaits High Court approval of its takeover of PTSB later this month.

]]><![CDATA[Lidl has moved into Irish mobile phone market. Can it save you money?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/23/every-lidl-helps-when-it-comes-to-saving-money-on-your-mobile-phone-costs/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/23/every-lidl-helps-when-it-comes-to-saving-money-on-your-mobile-phone-costs/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:44:11 +0000Earlier this month Lidl created quite a stir when it announced it had started selling something unexpected – and not just the jack hammers, blow torches and inflatable swimming pools that we have grown accustomed to finding in the middle aisles.

The new unexpected things that Lidl started selling was mobile phones – or at least access to the Irish mobile phone network.

The top line was quite alluring.

The first 100,000 people who signed up to Lidl Connect were promised a monthly charge of €8.99 for life. They were given the option of picking up a physical Sim card in any Lidl store for an additional €0.99 or selecting an eSim and completing their registration via the Lidl Plus app at no extra cost.

The monthly rolling plans require no long-term commitment and include unlimited 5G data, unlimited calls and texts to any Irish and UK network, 50GB of EU and UK roaming data and 100 international minutes per month to more than 38 countries.

People who decided to migrate to Lidl Connect were told they could keep their existing mobile numbers or choose new ones if they were so inclined.

But bells and whistles and portability aside, it was the price tag that got Lidl the most attention, although we should point out that its offering is not all that much cheaper than Tesco’s Sim-only deal, which costs a tenner a month.

Lidl Connect is, however, much cheaper than what many Irish mobile phone users who are on long-term contracts are accustomed to paying.

How much cheaper?

That is the interesting thing.

A typical bill-pay customer might be paying €50 a month – a price that might include a free handset every couple of years. Or might not.

Leaving aside the handset for a moment, a 20-year-old who chooses the €8.99 a month deal at Lidl and lives for the next 70 years and never leaves the German discounter will end up paying a total of €7,551.60 over the course of their – hopefully – long and happy life.

Were this notional 20-year-old to instead sign up to a monthly bill-pay deal with one of the State’s leading operators and live for the same 70 years without ever switching, the total cost of their mobile phone would come in at €42,000 in today’s money.

Now we know we are making a lot of assumptions here, not least that we will still be using money, mobile phones or indeed Lidl 70 years from now.

But you get the idea. Sim-only, pay-as-you-go deals are much cheaper than the alternative.

But despite the savings to be made, a great many people ignore them. Sometimes they don’t even know the savings are on the table.

The way the system works sometimes actively works against us. Mobile phone contracts often include a new phone as part of the initial deal and last for two years. A significant chunk of the monthly tariff over those two years is used to pay for the “free” handset that was given at the outset.

But under the terms and conditions of almost all bill-pay contracts, once the two years are up, you own the handset outright, so obviously the monthly cost should fall.

Only it doesn’t.

After the first two years, a mobile provider can offer you a new phone in return for a new contract.

But if you’re happy with your current handset or don’t get the offer or contact your provider to arrange a better deal – or switch to a different, cheaper provider – the company will keep charging the original monthly fee.

Actually, they might even charge more because, over the two years, as a bill pay customer you will most likely have been hit with two automatically-imposed price hikes. Virgin Mobile is an exception to this rule.

So, if you sign up to a two-year contract with a monthly payment of €50 and continue to pay in full after the contract ends, you’re giving the company at least €40 a month for absolutely nothing. That is €480 a year.

According to admittedly self-interested research published by Sky Mobile to coincide with its arrival in the Irish mobile market a couple of years ago, about 300,000 people in Ireland are overpaying each year.

If they all overpay by €40 a month, then Ireland is collectively wasting close to €150 million every single year.

Under ComReg rules, the mobile phone providers “must make you aware that your contract is coming to an end and that you may cancel your current plan”.

“Your provider should also send you ‘best tariff advice’ highlighting the best tariff, price plan or bundle, from your current service provider that suits your needs.”

No doubt that is done but if it is to make any difference you have to actually read the correspondence you are sent and we all know that is a big ask.

In a moderately ideal world, the price of your phone contract would automatically drop after two years to reflect what you are actually paying for, rather than what you were paying for at the start.

But our world is a long way from ideal, which is why you need to look after yourself.

If you own a phone outright, the cheapest thing to do is to hang on to it and request your current provider to unlock the device, allowing you to switch to a Sim-only plan with another provider, or with the likes of Lidl.

The switching process is not overly complicated, although it is not always free of complications, and you obviously get to hang on to your existing number.

As well as Lidl and Tesco Mobile there are also the likes of Sky Mobile, Clear Mobile and GoMo, all of which piggyback on the main providers’ networks, so the level of coverage should be comparable.

That is not the only way to save.

Are women in your workplace earning less? A new Government website lifts the lid

A lot of higher-priced contracts are sold with the promise of huge amounts of data. But most users rarely exceed the standard amounts on the table, particularly if they are good at connecting to free wifi when out and about.

Another easy money saving measure is a good haggle. Before your contract is due to end, work out what the alternatives are and then demand better value. If you are getting nowhere with the person you are speaking to, ask to talk to someone in their retention unit; they might be more receptive to your threats to leave.

More than half of under-12s have overnight access to smart devices, survey says

No matter who you are with or how much you are paying, do pay attention to roaming charges. Thankfully – because of our friends in Brussels – roaming charges are not the same money-grabbing gouging curse they once were (at least when you are using your phone across the EU) but if you are outside of the EU – or taking a ferry from Ireland to France, for instance – you could still be hit with a savagely high bill if you roam like you’re at home.

And do consider insurance. It can cost more than €10 a month but if you are prone to breaking or losing your phone, it can be money well spent. Before you sign up, check whether the contents insurance you have for your home covers personal possessions, as that might give you a safety net of sorts. If you do have specific mobile phone insurance and do change your handset, don’t assume the old policy will cover the new phone. It might not and that could see you paying for insurance on a phone you no longer have.

And if you are going Sim-only, consider buying second-hand. There are a lot of platforms offering refurbished handsets for a whole lot less than they cost new and even Apple sells refurbed phones. Just make sure you check the terms and conditions and have a degree of protection should things go wrong.

You can contact us at OnTheMoney@irishtimes.com with personal finance questions you would like to see us address. If you missed last week’s newsletter, you can read it here.

Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, traded around $114 (€100.72) a barrel, up almost 4 per cent this week, while West Texas Intermediate, the US benchmark, was above $100. Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed recent attacks on the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu, as well as deadly strikes on an oilfield and airport in the kingdom.

The flare-up threatens to widen hostilities around the Strait of Hormuz, where crude exports have recovered to near pre-war levels. Brent is up more than 85 per cent this year because of the US-Iran war, now approaching its ninth month, while refined-product prices have risen even faster, most notably diesel.

Higher oil prices dragged on European shares on Friday. The pan-European Stoxx 600 index was ⁠down 0.13 per cent in early trading, ‌after ‌logging ​its biggest one-day drop in three weeks on Thursday and putting ⁠the index on ​course for a weekly decline.

At the White House on Thursday, US president Donald Trump told reporters that the US has “knocked” out Iran and threatened to go “a little bit further”, without elaborating. The New York Times reported this week that the US and Israel have developed plans for renewed strikes against the Islamic Republic after the American midterm elections early next month.

“The latest geopolitical escalations are pointing to a more intensified strike on Iran, which is pushing crude higher throughout the price curve,” said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president for trading at BOK Financial Securities. Most traders expect oil prices to be higher for longer, he said.

The Yemen-based Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi Arabia in recent months. State-owned Aramco evacuated its Dhahran headquarters on Thursday and asked staff to work from home after an alarm, according to people familiar with the matter. The reason for the alarm was not immediately known.

While crude flows from the Gulf have recovered, oil-product shipments from the region remain constrained. That squeeze, along with intensifying Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, has prompted governments to tap stockpiles. Trump is also pushing measures to lower prices in advance of the midterm elections, including a diesel deal with Moscow.

Russia, meanwhile, is seeing some relief in its domestic fuel market, with gasoline and diesel production rising, Interfax reported, citing the government. Fuel inventories are also being replenished, it said. – Bloomberg, Reuters

]]>Aaron Schwartz<![CDATA[First-time buyers account for almost two-thirds of Irish mortgage transactions]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/first-time-buyers-account-for-almost-two-thirds-of-mortgage-transactions/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/first-time-buyers-account-for-almost-two-thirds-of-mortgage-transactions/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000First-time buyers continue to dominate the State’s mortgage market, accounting for almost two thirds of transactions.

The latest figures from Banking and Payments Federation Ireland (BPFI) indicate there were 8,164 first-time buyer mortgages drawn down in the third quarter.

This was “the highest Q3 volume since 2008”, the banking group noted.

Three Government-backed programmes – the Help to Buy scheme, First Home scheme and the Local Authority Home Loan scheme – are helping fuel demand for first-time buyer mortgages.

A total of 14,217 mortgages with a value of €4.6 billion were drawn down by all borrowers between July and September this year.

This represented a 13 per cent increase in volume terms and a 15.7 per cent increase in value compared with the same period last year.

First-time buyers remained the single largest segment by volume (57.4 per cent) and by value (58.3 per cent).

Re-mortgaging and switching volumes and values increased by 41.7 per cent and 50.9 per cent year on year respectively, the banking group said.

What you need to know about financing a new-build home

BPFI chief executive Brian Hayes said: “Our latest figures show continued momentum across the mortgage market, with growth in drawdowns across every customer segment during the third quarter of 2026.”

He noted there were 35,449 mortgage drawdowns valued at almost €11.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026, with volumes up by 8.2 per cent and values up by 12 per cent year on year.

“First-time buyers continue to drive the mortgage market, accounting for almost six in every 10 drawdowns,” Hayes said.

The BPFI said that 3,244 of first-time buyer mortgages drawn down in the third were for new properties, up 7.5 per cent year on year “and the highest Q3 level since 2007”.

The increase in new properties was driven by mortgages on new-build property purchases rather than self-builds, where first-time buyer volumes fell by 5.8 per cent year on year to 666.

The figure indicated that approvals activity also grew in September, up 13.3 per cent in volume and 17 per cent in value year on year, with growth recorded across both first-time buyer and mover purchase segments.

Opinion: Subsidies like Help to Buy are no longer needed as homebuyer demand weakens

Despite the increased activity, a recent report by the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland found that a first-time buyer couple with two incomes availing of the Government’s Help to Buy scheme still faced a considerable affordability gap when trying to buy a home in Dublin or surrounding counties.

It found that buying couples on a combined income of €113,000 with a 10 per cent deposit (and with the Central Bank’s mortgage rules) would face a shortfall of almost €25,000 in Kildare, €20,500 in Wicklow and €11,500 in Meath.

]]><![CDATA[EY chief Frank O’Keeffe: ‘We are well on our way to becoming a billion-euro business’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/ey-chief-frank-okeeffe-we-are-well-on-our-way-to-becoming-a-billion-euro-business/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/ey-chief-frank-okeeffe-we-are-well-on-our-way-to-becoming-a-billion-euro-business/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 04:16:00 +0000“This view is great but upstairs will knock your socks off,” says EY managing partner Frank O’Keeffe as he takes in the views of Dublin on a mild and sunny morning from the rooftop of its new headquarters at Wilton Park, alongside the Grand Canal.

He’s not wrong, though my socks survive the blast.

“Just look at the view,” he purrs.

The nearby Aviva Stadium looms large on one side, Liberty Hall can be seen on another and there are wonderful views in the distance of the Dublin mountains and the bay.

The rooftop has a few levels, with a small amphitheatre for outdoor gatherings, some neatly clipped lawns and a forest of colourful shrubs and trees.

It’s a statement investment by EY. So much so that O’Keeffe won’t disclose how many millions were spent on fit-out costs, only that it was delivered “on budget and on time”.

Two of the floors are an acre each in size, and the new HQ can accommodate 3,500 “colleagues and about 600 external guests” at any one time, O’Keeffe says.

On the ground floor, it has three meeting rooms that are available for use by the near 670 alumni of its successful and high profile EY Entrepreneur of the Year programme.

Totalling just under 18,000sq m (190,000 sq ft) of plush office space, it is about 50 per cent bigger than its previous, dated properties in the capital.

EY is very much in growth mode. When O’Keeffe took over as managing partner in 2018, the Big Four accounting firm had annual revenues of about €250 million on the island of Ireland. In the year to the end of June 2025, its fee income was €850 million.

O’Keeffe won’t be drawn on the figure for the year to the end of June 2026 but it’s expected to nudge €900 million.

“Business is good,” he says. “We are well on our way to reaching our strategic objective of becoming a billion euro turnover business over the next number of years.

“We changed our strategy last year because we were watching the world change, from a geopolitical perspective, from a technology and AI perspective and from a national versus global perspective.

“So we changed our strategy around IQ and EQ, all around behaviours. We have digitalised all of our business.

“We have pivoted around how we go to market. We make sure we have an industry lens and a sector lens in everything we do, not just a service lens.”

He describes how EY goes to “market together” with its alliance partners, namechecking Microsoft, SAP, Service Now and Snowflake.

“We became the Microsoft partner of the year for their full ecosystem. We did the exact same with SAP. We also decided that we would export a lot of our capability in Ireland into other [EY] member firms where they needed our support and our help.”

He cites the Nordic countries and the US as examples of where some of its key staff are deployed to work on projects for big clients of sister firms.

He says the Irish firm has spent a “significant amount of money” on training and upskilling its staff so it can deliver for clients.

This all feeds into a plan to achieve turnover of €1.3 billion by 2031, whichwould represent growth of about €400 million over the period.

More than half of Irish business leaders worried over ‘sophisticated cyber attacks’ by AI

O’Keeffe estimates that EY is the largest Big Four firm in the market, some 40 per cent bigger than KPMG, in second place.

EY employs 5,600 staff on the island (it has 157 equity partners), with 4,400 in the Republic and 3,500 allocated to Dublin. About 2,000 of its staff were not born in Ireland and some 100 nationalities are represented at the firm.

Which brings us to the impact of artificial intelligence on EY’s business, specifically the potential impact on its graduate programme and overall headcount.

“An awful lot of this has yet to be determined and figured out,” says O’Keeffe, while adding that the firm has the largest AI and data analytics practice of any professional services firm on the island, with a team of 350 people.

Within EY, he says it has “embedded AI tooling in our own methodologies in how we actually perform our work on behalf of clients”.

“In our insurance business, we’ve got very specific tools. You could even go into journal entry testing or predictive analytics and sample sizing right through to diligence and corporate finance and also into tax. They are all our own tools.”

When search engines came out, people said there will be no need for professional services. [AI] is no different and there will be winners and losers ... things will change but we will continue to grow

Frank O’Keeffe

It is also using Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude on a day-to-day basis. “We have nearly one and a half thousand technology consultants that you could tag to being AI ... but everybody else is using AI tools and processes and licenses to make sure that we do the most effective roles to support our clients. And we believe we’re ahead of the our competition.”

Amid tales of hallucination, does he trust the accuracy of AI tools?

“We have very rigorous quality control measures when it comes to anything that we produce for the external marketplace. Everything gets reviewed by a human ... we work together as teams to ensure we’re using the technology in the right way and that we’ve got the right processes and controls and oversight in place to ensure we can stand over everything we deliver into the market.”

PwC published ‘thought leadership’ reports marred by AI hallucinations

He acknowledges that mistakes can and probably will happen, adding that the firm needs to remain “vigilant” in terms of the quality of information it uses and disseminates.

He says EY took on 400 new graduates in September across the island, a “very similar number” to a year ago. “And we’re currently assessing the business need for 2027.”

He’s not convinced that AI will replace graduates in huge numbers. “We’ve always invested in the next generation of talent an we’ll continue to do that as a significant employer of graduates.”

He says today’s graduates have a head start in terms of their abilities on digitalisation, AI and technology, meaning they could rise up the ranks more quickly than would have been the case in the past.

Will the graduate number always be around the 400 mark?

“Nobody can give you that answer. It has yet to be determined. The market is shifting, the way of work is shifting and we have to determine what that will look like over the next number of years.”

Graduate recruitment slowdown by firms like KPMG in UK sends shiver down spine of south Co Dublin

Looking out five years, will EY still have 5,600 staff? “At least, he says. “But I also think the ways of working will change and what our people will be doing will be different. If you remember, when the search engines came out, people said there will be no need for professional services. This is no different and there will be winners and losers ... things will change but we will continue to grow.”

O’Keeffe is a glass-half-full person and is confident on the future growth prospects for the Irish economy. EY provides audit or advisory services to many of the big multinationals that operate here.

Does he worry that the recent corporation tax windfalls are at risk by one or more of the tech or pharma giants pulling out?

“That’s something that the Government and the IDA need to be really conscious of,” he says. “They need to stay really close to all of the individual companies and they need to explain the attractiveness of Ireland.

“The Government is very pro-business but they need to stay close to what are the issues that those corporation face globally.”

Ireland’s corporate tax advantage is over. So what’s the plan?

He also makes the point that Ireland needs to be seen as a welcoming place for senior executives and other “talent” that those same multinationals employ here.

“We need to make clear that we’re a welcoming country with humility, which has brilliant talent. Only six generations ago our people had to be leave this island because there was nothing here for our talent.

“Now we have an opportunity to ... bring people from around the world to Ireland. But we cannot do that if we show any signs of xenophobia within our country, and we’ve seen it in pockets, especially in 2025.”

Is the Government right to tighten the rules on immigration?

“We have to be very mindful of people who have already committed to building their lives here and naturalising themselves. We have to be very clever on who comes here for the benefit of the country. That’s a tricky balance for the Government, no doubt. But we need to attract high-end jobs so that we have the best talent coming to the country, because they will also share their experiences and help others develop and grow to that level of talent. We need to make sure that we’re not losing our ability ... to bring the right people that this country needs to continue its success in the years ahead.”

Unlike most of its rivals, there is no term mandate in place for EY managing partners. O’Keeffe has been in situ for eight years now. Does he intend to see the new five-year strategy plan through?

“I hope so. I have all the energy in the world but that will be determined by my fellow partners. The time has flown by and we’ve had so much change from Brexit to Covid to wars, you name it.

“I wake up every morning with lots of energy and still believe I’ll be doing it [the job] tomorrow, next year and hopefully the year after.”

CV

Name: Frank O’Keeffe.

Age: 53.

Job: Managing Partner, EY Ireland.

Family: Married to Susan, four children.

Hobbies: Golf, GAA, rugby.

Something you might expect: “Passionate about the interconnected forces of people, business, technology and the geopolitics shaping our world.”

Something that might surprise: “For all the seriousness of my day job, I don’t take myself too seriously and I’m usually happiest when there’s a bit of fun and laughter around.”

Leadership style: “I’d describe it as open, collaborative and straightforward. I try to give people the trust and space to be at their best. I’m a big believer in listening, staying curious and bringing people with me. And I’ve always thought a bit of humour helps, particularly when things get challenging.”

Kilkenny Design

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Trump is about to discover the political cost of inflation]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The great slayer of political careers – inflation – has come for Donald Trump.

They have averaged over $4 a gallon for a record 169 days, a timeline that runs concurrent with the Iran war. The average cost of gas in California, the most expensive state, has been over $6 since late September.

Car ownership is a necessity in many parts of the US, with motorists spending on average two-thirds more on fuel than their European counterparts. That’s why fuel costs are such a flashpoint.

The country’s 196,000 gas stations and their price billboards serve as a daily reminder of Trump’s failed war aims, a political burden he now carries into the midterm elections. Polls suggest he will lose big.

US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections

The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey indicates Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31 per cent. It was 44 per cent at the same point in his first term.

More worrying for Trump’s avowedly pro-business administration is that more than two-thirds (68 per cent) of voters disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37 per cent of republicans.

Asked which party they would vote ⁠for if the elections were held today, some ​47 per cent of registered voters chose Democrats, while 35 per cent chose republicans.

The 12-point advantage in favour of Democrats ​is the widest in the current election cycle and could, if translated into actual votes, see the Democrats seize control of both houses, the House of Representatives and the Senate.

What are the US midterms? A visual guide

This would hobble Trump’s presidency as Democrats would be in a position to block cabinet and judicial appointments while having subpoena powers to investigate the administration.

The top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia of California, says he will prioritise the examination of Trump’s family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering, and how US health secretary Robert Kennedy jnr has handled vaccines.

US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent (in annual terms) in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This was faster than the annual growth in wages (3 per cent), meaning real wages are falling.

Trump’s big mistake has been to dismiss this marker or at least be insensitive to it, repeatedly telling voters that the economy is great and that they’ve never had it so good.

“We have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” he repeatedly says at rallies.

To be fair, the US economy is faring better than many had predicted in the wake of his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025. Unemployment has been at or below 4.5 per cent for 60 consecutive months, a postwar record. Consumer spending remains solid while business investment is being fuelled by the AI boom.

But Trump is falling into the same trap as his predecessor, Joe Biden, in talking up the macroeconomy when consumers and households are being screwed by the micro one: prices.

Jame Carville’s’s famous maxim, “It’s the economy, stupid”, might need to be refined to “It’s the price economy, stupid”, to highlight what matters most to voters in the 2020s.

The Irish Government has learned not to make political capital out of its turbocharged GDP numbers or its windfall taxes, as it only antagonises households in the grip of a price squeeze.

But Trump can’t help himself.

US inflation peaked at 9 per cent in June 2022 as the reopening of the economy after the pandemic led to a burst in price growth. A year later it had fallen to 3.1 per cent and by Trump’s election win in November 2024, it was down to 2.6 per cent. It had been expected to fall to the Federal Reserve’s target rate of 2 per cent by the end of 2025, paving the way for growth-affirming interest rate cuts.

But Trump destroyed that trajectory by imposing tariffs on imported goods. Inflation stopped falling and started to rise again, hitting 3 per cent in September 2025.

Even with the tariffs, US inflation would probably have slowed again this year if the US leader hadn’t gone to war with Iran, triggering a spike in global oil prices.

This has not just driven up petrol prices but also the cost of diesel, the fuel needed to transport everything.

The full ramifications of Trump’s war can be seen through the prism of producer prices, which surged by 6.3 per cent in September. This will translate into further consumer price inflation in the coming months.

High inflation is also resulting in upward pressure on interest rates, further anchoring household spending and Trump’s poll ratings.

Trump’s political shtick has always been to proclaim everything he touches gold. It won’t wash this time.

]]><![CDATA[Central Bank inquiry made ‘fundamental errors’ in former PTSB chief tracker mortgage case]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/central-bank-inquiry-made-fundamental-errors-in-former-ptsb-chief-tracker-mortgage-case/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/central-bank-inquiry-made-fundamental-errors-in-former-ptsb-chief-tracker-mortgage-case/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:55:20 +0000A tribunal has confirmed that former PTSB chief executive David Guinane has won an appeal against a Central Bank of Ireland inquiry sanctioning him for a role played in the State’s tracker mortgage scandal.

The Irish Financial Services Appeals Tribunal (Ifsat) said that the sole inquiry member, Peter Hinchliffe, made errors of law that were so fundamental that they negated his decision last year that Guinane be fined €80,000 and reprimanded.

The tribunal concluded in a decision published on Thursday that Hinchliffe “erred in law”, acted beyond what was established by case law elsewhere, “failed to give fair notice of certain issues”, and “failed to give reasons for his decision”.

“Moreover, it held that the errors of law in the inquiry decision were manifest from the text and were fundamental so as to deprive the decision of its basis,” said the tribunal, chaired by chaired by former Supreme Court judge John MacMenamin.

Its conclusion still needs to be confirmed by the High Court. The Central Bank said it does not plan to appeal it.

The Irish Times first reported on the conclusion of the appeal last month.

Former PTSB chief wins appeal over tracker mortgage sanction

“This deeply flawed process, which has cost millions in taxpayer funds, has had a profound effect on my family and on my career,” said Guinane in a statement on Thursday afternoon.

“With this now-discredited allegation, the Central Bank tried to single me out as a scapegoat. It is extraordinary that I was the only individual to be subject to a formal inquiry in respect of the tracker issue.”

Ifsat said that the Central Bank should pay Guinane’s legal costs for the inquiry and appeal, including his €5,000 appeal fee.

It rejected an application by PTSB, a notice party in the case, for costs. PTSB paid a €21 million fine in 2019 for its role in the industry-wide tracker mortgage scandal.

Hinchliffe emphasised last year there was “no finding of dishonesty against Mr Guinane” and that he “did not form an intention to harm or take advantage of customers”. Guinane was also entitled to receive better support from within the wider Irish Life & Permanent Group, of which PTSB was a part at the time, he added.

The inquiry centred on a special condition in some PTSB tracker mortgages offered during the pre-crash property boom. This required customers who moved for a period to a fixed rate to instruct the bank afterwards to put them back on a tracker rate or another fixed product. Otherwise, they would default to a standard variable rate.

The ambiguous wording of the condition led to questions in early 2009 about whether a customer opting to go back on to a tracker rate was entitled to their original margin over the European Central Bank rate, or a higher margin then on offer from PTSB.

The bank adopted a strategy in January 2009, on the basis of legal advice, to only put customers who requested the original rate – or complained – on the more favourable rate. The Central Bank said Guinane signed off on the strategy when he responded to the plan, when advanced by a colleague via email in January 2009, with the words, “okay to that”.

Guinane testified during an inquiry hearing in early 2024 that while he did not remember events surrounding the decision, he understood the email to mean – based on having reviewed documents – that “any customer” coming out of the fixed rate would “go back to their original rate”. The email only contained a summary of the legal advice.

The grounds for the Central Bank’s decision to hold the inquiry were that Guinane knew and understood the strategy.

However, Ifsat said Hinchliffe reframed the allegation by removing “those critical elements of knowledge and approval”.

Instead, Hinchliffe criticised Guinane’s “failure” to ask certain questions, to make follow-up enquiries, or to take other steps which might have shown him what was happening to PTSB customers.

“The meaning of the allegation, as originally notified to the appellant was fundamentally altered in the ultimate decision,” Ifsat said.

The Ifsat decision raises questions about whether the Central Bank will still go after other bankers suspected of having played a role in the tracker mortgage scandal.

Ifsat’s conclusion marks another major setback for the regulator’s post-crisis vetting and enforcement activities.

Ifsat was previously highly critical in 2024 of a Central Bank refusal to approve a board nominee for a fund, saying the decision-making process was “flawed” and denied the individual fair procedures “at every stage”.

The Central Bank was also found in a High Court ruling, published in April, to have badly handled an enforcement investigation into a funds industry executive, saying it was “irretrievably tainted” by errors. The bank committed to learning lessons and changing procedures as a result of both cases.

]]>Gabby Jones<![CDATA[Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/22/workplace-conflict-costs-millions-annually-but-what-can-be-done-to-remedy-this-problem/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/22/workplace-conflict-costs-millions-annually-but-what-can-be-done-to-remedy-this-problem/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 04:56:00 +0000When I moved here from New York more than three decades ago, I became the default complainer in restaurants. It wasn’t my choice; others expected me to give out for them. I found it strange that even when an Irish friend’s meal was inedible and the service lacking, they’d say everything was okay: “Fine, grand, lovely, thanks.”

If they wanted to express their dissatisfaction with the food, they’d switch plates with me and try to persuade me to gripe on their behalf. Initially, it was amusing, but then it became annoying. Why couldn’t they just complain themselves? Why was this such a big deal to them?

As I only learned after years working and living here – despite being raised abroad by a mother from Carlow and a dad from Dublin – Irish culture is polite and indirect. Avoiding conflict and saving face is a big part of society and often informs how people communicate, or don’t.

Culturally, we know that our strength comes from togetherness and mutual care. Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine: as we live in one another’s shelter. Although we’ve become a more individualistic society in the last 50 years, much of our communalist culture remains in our behaviours and attitudes.

William Corless, a workplace mediator and coach, says cultural norms follow us into the office. When it comes to conflict at work or anywhere, he says, the Irish approach is to avoid it nearly at all costs.

“We’re a land of a thousand welcomes, so we have to be nice,” he says. “But it has to seep out somewhere.” It finds its way into the post-meeting huddle where people are whispering to one another and asking ‘what was that all about?’ instead of complaining constructively. Then it might grow into gossip, then later into a culture of ‘quiet quitting’ or people leaving. In many cases, this can feel more comfortable than addressing an issue head-on.

Both head-on avoidance and conflict itself can be very expensive, professionally and personally, if not well managed. Data indicates that workplace conflict, interpersonal mistreatment and work-related distress result in hundreds of millions of euro in lost productivity annually, plus direct legal awards and reduced performance and efficiency across Irish organisations.

The estimated overall value of lost productivity due to workplace conflict is €239.3 million, with €187.6 million in the private sector and €51.8 million in the public sector, according to the Value of Lost Productivity from Workplace Bullying in Ireland, a 2020 study by NUI Galway’s John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan. Across the entire economy, absenteeism from conflict results in approximately 1.42 million missed days in the private sector and 276,473 days in the public sector annually, says the report.

Employees who reported that they were bullied were considerably more likely to report that they were often or always stressed, while bad and very bad relationships between management and staff were also significantly associated with greater stress, particularly for female employees. That’s according to Bullying and Work-Related Stress in the Irish Workplace, a 2019 study from NUI Galway, by the same researchers plus Michael McDermott and Sharon Walsh.

Remote and hybrid working can also increase the potential for conflict as some of the signals we rely on – body language, physical presence – go missing. Corless likens poor communication and conflict to a screen with missing pixels. We fill in the gaps, but sometimes we fill them in the wrong way and we tend to assume negative intent because we are wired to protect ourselves, he says.

Conflict isn’t always bad and, if well managed, constructive disagreement is the sign of an engaged workforce. High-performing teams aren’t those that never fight – they’re the ones who learn to listen to each other and reset the fastest after disagreements.

When there is an issue, managers carry much of the weight in resolving both indirect and direct conflict. Even so, many find there is little organisational, structural support or training to help them address the problem.

Katie Muldoon, author of Mind Your Self: How Leaders can Integrate AI without Disintegrating Humans, says teams should agree the ground rules together before conflict has a chance to arise.

Start with agreeing on principles, not rules. “A principle is: if we were to do the opposite, would it still be reasonable?” she says. We treat each other kindly is a rule, because nobody would argue for the reverse. Whereas saying we meet in person by default is a principle, because there are good reasons to sometimes do otherwise. When someone wants to break a principle, the team already has a shared reference point for that conversation. Leaders can still make the call, she says, but they should explain it and acknowledge the frustration it may cause.

“You might also ask each individual, ‘what are we here to do as a team?’ You may be surprised to find several different answers, and this may be the original root of conflict in the group.”

Consistency is extremely important for team cohesion too. What unsettles teams is unpredictability, says Muldoon, like “the boss who is warm on Monday and furious on Tuesday”.

She suggests managers think through their communication based on a driving analogy – mirror, signal, manoeuvre. Look in the mirror: what does the team need today? Signal the change in tone. Then manoeuvre and explain why. If, for example, the company’s share price has just dropped, you might be focusing on that when in reality people may be worrying about their jobs and not listening to your plan at all.

Rapport pays off when things get heated. If you know a colleague, Muldoon says, you can tell whether difficult behaviour is a state – a bad day – or a trait. “When we don’t know each other, we avoid conflict. And when it goes underneath the surface, it simmers.” It emerges as missed tasks and skipped meetings. Psychological safety matters here too. “A high-performing team doesn’t make fewer mistakes,” she says. “They learn from them quicker because they can talk about it.”

Managing conflict: Top tips:

1. Put formal structures in place for issues like sexual harassment and bullying;

2. Agree team conflict resolution principles and rules from the start. Formal rules are how we work together. Principles can act as guardrails if disagreement arises. Informal structures like weekly team check-ins, shared learning sessions, and one-to-one meetings set us up for success;

3. Repair before resolving: acknowledge the emotions and manage assumptions first so that tensions can decrease and thinking can re-emerge;

4. Determine if it’s a state or trait. Was the engagement you had with someone indicative of a hard day or a character flaw? Someone may just have been having an awful day, so reflect on your assumptions before reacting;

5. Have the courage to speak up. If team members don’t learn how to disagree constructively, then feelings and resentments get pushed down, and this is where real tension simmers. It’s best to speak up and get it resolved early ... and learn how to complain about your own dinner too.

  • Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

Gross national debt is due to rise from €208 billion this year to €236 billion by 2029, but of course there will be increased cash assets on the other side in the two funds.

The key debate is just how volatile the Irish public finances outlook is. The Department of Finance estimates that “potentially transient” corporation tax now accounts for around half of all tax from this heading – about €18.8 billion this year rising to almost €23 billion next year.

But it would probably require an “event” – say a big drop in payments from one or two of the big payers – to draw attention to Ireland.

It wasn’t the internet that killed the old cultural order, it was U2

“One of the foundations of Apple is predictability, and with the free U2 album all of a sudden iTunes was behaving in an entirely new and unexplained way. If it’s a U2 album today, what might it be tomorrow?” he tells The Irish Times.

One of the secrets of Apple’s success is simplicity, he says. Simple solutions are more effective, more resilient and easier to understand. They reduce friction and they help cement relationships with customers.

Apple has mastered both simplicity and the “jobs to be done” idea that people don’t purchase products, they hire them to do a specific task. The iPhone packs all the functionality you need daily with a phone, a camera, a music player, a browser and apps. AirPods pair seamlessly and remove the tangle of traditional wired earbuds. The iPod was the first mass market product to come fully charged, a small tweak at the manufacturing stage that delighted customers. In the same manner, bundling a little screwdriver into the Nest thermostat removed a friction in what was otherwise a simple installation. As Tony Faddell, the creator of both the iPod and Nest, puts it: “It may not be your fault that the customer doesn’t have the right screwdriver to hand, but that won’t stop them feeling bad about your product.”

Apple’s $5tn milestone comes with a hefty price tag

Not all additions are welcome, as the U2 experience shows. When the iTunes Music Store launched, West suggested adding a £10 iTunes gift card to the box of every new iPhone and iPod sold. Steve Jobs hated the idea and shot it down. This was a battle of philosophies between a team with a tactical marketing plan versus Apple’s devotion to the user experience.

“It was a distracting call to action that would force the customer to pause their emotional journey with their new product and think about a separate transaction,” West says.

Apple is famous for this type of exceptionalism, and Jobs personified it, with his genius, volatility and creation of a culture of intense secrecy at the corporation. West’s 16-year period at Apple covered both Jobs’ and his successor Tim Cook’s tenures at the top, with their radically different styles.

“It’s no secret that at times Steve could be abrasive, rude and extremely direct,” West says. “At the same time, everyone who worked directly with him will tell you that was almost immediately forgiven because it wasn’t personal; it was in pursuit of greatness and he more than proved that his methods led to greatness.

“It’s very easy to look at the headlines about the things that were launched under Steve Jobs and miss the innovations that changed the world, but let’s not forget that Tim raised Apple’s value by around 14-fold,” he says. “It’s a fun game all right to imagine what world-changing products Apple might have launched had Steve still been with us, but I think the more adult business perspective is to imagine what mediocre, unpolished products might have been released by Apple had anyone other than Tim Cook been leading it.

“People mistake innovation for creating something new. Apple has always seen innovation as being about making things better. Inevitably, the process of innovation involves developing ideas that ultimately never come to market. A classic example is Project Titan, Apple’s secretive plan for a self-driving electric car, which was reportedly abandoned in 2024 after around a decade of development.

West says that a cornerstone of Apple’s success over the years has been what Jobs used to call “ownership of the whole widget”, and he feels it would not have been feasible for Apple to manufacture its own cars. “Apple was going to have to surrender a great deal of control over how the car was made and that was always going to weaken its ability to develop something great in the same way it can with iPods or iPhones.”

On the culture of secrecy at Apple, West feels that this is a combination of normal competitive practice and Apple’s long-standing desire to make exciting surprise announcements.

“I had absolutely no visibility at all regarding the car project, for example. I didn’t need to know, so I didn’t know. Secrecy can seem arrogant, but it is a very competitive business with other companies looking at your strategy and adjusting theirs accordingly.”

In the area of artificial intelligence, Apple has taken a strategic bet to let others lead in the creation of AI models. West says his hunch is the major battle here may not be about who has the most powerful models but who can use AI to solve the most problems for people and that Apple may be on the money here. “I think it will be a winning strategy. West’s book provides some interesting colour about the inside of Apple, while never compromising his relationship with his former employer who he clearly retains huge affection for. He returns constantly to the theme of simplicity. In a world of information overload, this is one of the keys to a winning business strategy, he concludes.

An aviation maintenance firm which dismissed one of its co-founders while he was out of work sick following a breakdown in relations at the firm during a €1.2 million pay dispute has been awarded €41,000 at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

Gerry Burke secured the award against Magellan Aviation Services Ltd on foot of a complaint under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977, following the termination of his employment in August 2023 after 33 years at the firm.

Burke was a co-founder and managing director of the company prior to its acquisition in 2013 by the Tokyo-headquartered Marubeni Corporation, the WRC heard.

His base salary in that job was €80,000 – later increased to €88,000 – with health insurance, pension contribution and a contractual provision for a €305,000-a-year bonus, bringing his total annual remuneration to €369,786, his lawyers said.

A preliminary objection by the company submitted that the Unfair Dismissals Act did not apply, arguing that Burke lived in Malta, carried out his work “entirely outside” Ireland, and had his salary paid free of Irish income tax. This argument was rejected.

The company received tax advice in 2022 that it was unlawful to pay Burke his salary without deducting either Irish or Maltese tax, it was submitted.

It sought to “regularise” the situation with a new contract increasing Burke’s pay and requiring he pay income tax in Malta, but Burke rejected this, the company submitted further.

Burke said in evidence that the allegations of “tax evasion” levelled at him by the firm were “thrown in to discredit [him] and put a cloud over his reputation”. He was “tax-compliant in Ireland and in Malta”, he said.

His position was that he had contacted Marubeni’s compliance department in 2022 with what his lawyers submitted was a protected disclosure concerning the sale of the company, management practices, and certain pay and contract matters, the tribunal was told.

It was Burke’s case that an investigation into the pay and contract matters proceeded first, with a directive issued from Marubeni that Burke receive a 15 per cent pay rise, which was not actioned, his lawyers submitted further.

The company’s managing director, Niall Duggan, said that when he put the proposal to Burke at a meeting in Zurich, the complainant “suggested that he would move to Dubai”.

Duggan added that Burke “intended to sue [the company] if it took action to ensure that it complied with [Malta’s] tax legislation”.

Burke agreed he had threatened an injunction but said that without the firm sharing its tax advice with him, he could not reasonably agree to the company’s plans to establish a company in Malta and make him an employee there.

In 2023, Duggan said, “matters became increasingly fractious”, with Burke initiating a High Court action in Ireland and seeking to escalate the dispute to the leadership of the Marubeni Corporation in Japan.

In March that year, Burke underwent “serious surgery”, his legal team submitted. The actions of Magellan caused him “stress and strain” and delayed his recovery, it was further submitted.

After about five months’ absence due to sick leave, the company terminated Burke’s employment on the basis of disability, the tribunal noted.

There was “an express contractual provision under which an executive is automatically deemed to have a disability following an extended absence from work due to ill-health” in Burke’s employment contract, the adjudication officer noted.

Although Burke sought reinstatement as his preferred remedy for the dismissal, his legal papers calculated his total losses at more than €1.2 million, the WRC recorded.

The WRC noted that Burke had alleged non-payment of salary going back to 2020, and had initiated separate proceedings in the High Court.

Ruling the dismissal unfair, adjudicator Ewa Sobanska wrote: “I cannot accept that other matters, some of them still remaining unresolved, had no impact on the respondent’s decision to dismiss [Burke], Sobanska wrote.

She was not satisfied the termination arose “wholly or mainly” due to any question of Burke’s capability, she wrote.

However, she found she could not order reinstatement on the basis of “fractious relationships” and “tension between the parties”.

Sobanska wrote that €41,434.08, about six months’ base salary, was a “just and equitable” award for the dismissal.

This was because she could not take Burke’s claimed bonus payments into account, and she regarded his efforts to seek new work to be “inadequate”.

Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors. Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley.

“AI has got so good that you can do so much with so little these days,” she said. “We need more people on the go-to-market front, that’s an area we could hire tomorrow. By the end of next year we are probably looking at a team of around 15 people.”

The company was born from a meeting between Hughes, who is a law graduate, and Dolphin through an NDRC founder weekend at Dogpatch Labs in 2024. Dolphin had been through the probate process, which is paper-heavy, following the death of his father.

Hughes said her experience of working in the industry matched Dolphin’s. That posed a simple question: why are highly trained legal professionals spending so much time retyping information?

The duo founded the company as Simple Probate, with Noonan subsequently coming on board as the third cofounder, bringing his experience of working with legal technology company Clio to the start-up.

Initially focused on Irish law firms, the company changed tack and focused on the US market, which was faster to adopt the platform.

Estatemin partnered with Clio and now supports law firms across all 50 US states. It has grown revenue 20 per cent month on month, with companies using the platform managing more than $770 million (€685 million) in estate value.

“We are growing quickly right now,” Hughes said. “We are always looking ahead and getting ready for that next round.”

   <title>Gesetz gegen SLAPP-Klagen vorgelegt</title>
   <description>Im Rahmen des jüngst vorgestellten Medienpakets hat die Regierung ein Gesetz gegen die Einschüchterung durch SLAPP-Klagen angekündigt und nun in Begutachtung geschickt. Eine Reform des Medienrechts soll zudem missbräuchliche Abmahnwellen stoppen. Im Vorfeld gab es bereits Kritik, etwa an zu langen Zeiträumen für das Löschen von Kommentaren. Justizministerin Anna Sporrer (SPÖ) kündigte an, entsprechende Inputs prüfen zu wollen.</description>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws.

However, the demonstrations, which took place on the sixth anniversary of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) ruling that introduced a near-total abortion ban, were nowhere near the scale of the massive protests that emerged back in 2020.

Było deszczowo, ale nie brakowało ludzi i emocji. Rzeszów pokazał czerwoną kartkę za aborcję rządzącej koalicji. pic.twitter.com/oJo8BiWXxS

— Paweł Preneta (@pawelpreneta) October 22, 2026

In Warsaw, a few hundred people gathered in the rain outside parliament, reported broadcaster RMF. Many held up red cards, a symbol used by the protesters to warn the government that it could be thrown out of power at next year’s parliamentary elections.

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party.

In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health.

 

However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition.

Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear.

Parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland's abortion laws

One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling that introduced a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise helping women in obtaining unlawful abortions https://t.co/nVj8SQVIsv

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2026

In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, around 1,000 people attended Thursday’s protest, according to police estimates cited by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Among the placards and banners was one showing Tusk with an extended, Pinocchio-style nose.

“It’s sad that we have to engage in this fight again,” said one of the organisers. “For so long, they ignored us, only coming when they needed votes. Now let’s show that we can’t be ignored.”

In Katowice, around 300 people gathered, according to the Polish Press Agency (PAP). In Poznań, around 400 or so protesters marched to the local headquarters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, where they placed a symbolic red card and waved banners saying “You deceived Poland”.

Czerwona kartka za aborcje. W #Lodz w proteście w strugach deszczu protestuje kilkadziesiąt osób @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/okU7QjnhFw

— Mateusz Szkudlarek (@m_szkudlarek) October 22, 2026

The 2020 TK abortion ruling triggered the largest protests seen in Poland since the communist era, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets. That anger is seen as having played a major role in PiS losing power to Tusk’s coalition in 2023.

Opinion polls consistently show that most Poles want the abortion law to be liberalised, though there remain divisions over whether there should be a return to the pre-2021 status quo or a move even further, to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

In autumn 2027, parliamentary elections will take place, deciding who governs Poland for the next four years. Opinion polls currently show a fairly even split in support between Tusk’s coalition and the right-wing opposition.

Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year.

The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself.

Warto przypomnieć:
▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości.
▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv

— Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026

Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons.

After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused.

On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then.

Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week.

"Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026

On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway.

The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban.

Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition.

 

Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN.

The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”.

Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty.

A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”.

However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026

The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”.

In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations.

Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia.

Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states.

The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies.

Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades.

During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”.

📍 New Delhi | Premier @donaldtusk spotkał się z Premierem Indii @narendramodi. pic.twitter.com/Y9HPLQsvf4

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 22, 2026

Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies.

Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20.

“The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said.

Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.”

 

Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market.

Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”.

“Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.”

However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals.

The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible".

"Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility.

To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations.

Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people.

The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors.

Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS).

Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026

The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations.

Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War.

“In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”.

The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.

]]> How will recent scandals affect Polish politics? https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/22/how-will-recent-scandals-affect-polish-politics/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 09:56:48 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105869 Aleks Szczerbiak Political scandals now rarely have the dramatic impact they once did.]]>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.
