PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him.

However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”.

The speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, called the comments “scandalous”, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk read out a message sent to him by a Polish army medic who was serving in Afghanistan when the last of 44 Polish soldiers who died there was declared dead.

Chciałbym, żeby te słowa dotarły do naszych sojuszników, żeby już nigdy więcej nikt nie lekceważył wysiłku naszych żołnierzy. pic.twitter.com/gGJkh4Gnft

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 20, 2026

The controversy stemmed from a speech the US defence secretary gave to US military cadets in Tennessee on Saturday. Hegseth referred to his time serving as a US Army officer in Afghanistan, where he recalled that the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) headquarters had flags from over 50 countries.

“Except,” Hegseth said, “there were maybe five [countries] that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that actually, by the end, were involved in kinetic operations. In fact, the patch ‘ISAF’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting.'”

The comments earned quick reproach from Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, who aimed a message at Hegseth on social media, saying: “Tell that to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province.”

Tell that, Mr @SecWar, to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province. https://t.co/vm4TM0sMJO

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 18, 2026

On Tuesday, the remarks earned even stronger reproach from Czarzasty, who is the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, and the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of the groups that forms Poland’s ruling coalition.

At a press conference, Czarzasty said that Hegseth’s “scandalous” comments are “harmful to the families of Polish soldiers and to Polish national pride”.

He also criticised President Karol Nawrocki – an opponent of the government and conservative ally of Donald Trump – for not condemning Hegseth’s remarks.

It is “an insult to Polish soldiers” that Nawrocki, who serves as commander-in-chief, “is unable to stand up for their dignity and the dignity of those who died”, declared Czarzasty.

To skandaliczne, że prezydent Polski boi się potępić polityków amerykańskich za brak szacunku do polskich żołnierzy, którzy zginęli w Afganistanie. pic.twitter.com/uyv54yDvrI

— Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) October 20, 2026

Later on Tuesday, Tusk read out to his cabinet a text message he said he had received from a former military medic, whom he did not name.

“Please stand up for soldiers, I beg you,” wrote the medic. “During my tour in Afghanistan, we confirmed the death of the last Polish casualty, a platoon sergeant whose wife was pregnant in Poland at the time.”

“I received a medal from the Americans for helping them, for treating Americans. I didn’t have to do that. We treated them with our own Polish medicines,” they added.

Tusk then added his own remarks, stating: “I would like these words to reach our allies. So that no one will ever again downplay the efforts of our soldiers. Wherever our allies, including our closest ally, the Americans, have needed our participation, Polish soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with them.”

Tusk also referenced Nawrocki’s silence on the matter. “Frankly, I was also counting on the president speaking out on this matter. But it seems I miscalculated.”

 

Tusk is the first European head of government to directly criticise Hegseth’s remarks, although a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham did say on Monday that it was “wrong to diminish the role” of British personnel, 457 of whom died in Afghanistan.

Of the 3,621 coalition deaths during the war in Afghanistan, around two thirds were Americans (2,461). The rest came from 31 different countries, with Poland’s 44 fatalities the seventh most of any nation.

Hegseth’s remarks are not the first time that the Trump administration has caused anger in Poland by downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan. In January, Trump himself suggested that other countries had “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines”.

That prompted General Roman Polko, who commanded Poland’s GROM special forces unit in Iraq and Afghanistan, to call the US president “a coward who has never been on the front lines”.

The former commander of Poland's special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan has condemned Donald Trump for questioning the contribution of America's allies

"This is the cynicism of a coward who hasn’t been on the front lines himself," said General @PolkoRoman https://t.co/kElkAO5qX4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 23, 2026

The Polish government has also clashed with the US on other issues. In January, Tusk joined other European leaders in calling for Greenland’s sovereignty to be respected, following Trump’s calls for the island to be brought under US control.

The following month, Tusk declared that Poland would not be a “vassal” of the US and suggested that Nawrocki wanted Poland to be too subservient to Washington. Czarzasty has twice this year clashed with the US ambassador over critical remarks he made towards Trump.

However, at the same time, the Polish government has sought to maintain positive relations with Washington, given the United States’ role as Poland’s most important security partner. In June, Poland formally requested that the US establish a new permanent military base on its territory.

Hegseth himself has praised Poland, calling it a “model ally” last year. The US State Department this month also announced that it was pushing for Poland to be allowed to join the G20 “as soon as possible”, pointing to its “growing leadership position in the international arena”.

The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation.

The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted.

Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures.

Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia.

Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU.

This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace.

What appears to be a drone exploded…

— Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026

On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object.

President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”.

Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace.

“I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT.

 

However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”.

Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country.

In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”.

Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”.

We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia.

We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have…

— Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026

Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian.

“We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.”

The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was.

Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming.

On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself.

It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place.

London Irish are targeting a return to the English professional pyramid next season after being acquired by rugby-loving Essex energy entrepreneur Steve Daniels.

Gamechanger Investments, led by Daniels, has bought the name, brand and associated intellectual property relating to the historic club, which went out of business in 2023, from Kyle Jordan, son of late Formula 1 legend Eddie, and Daniel McKeown.

They plan to resume pro rugby in 2027 and it is understood they had hoped to become the first English team to enter the United Rugby Championship, which features teams from Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Italy and South Africa.

Those ambitions met with resistance from within the game, so they are expected instead to aim for a place in the Champ, English rugby’s second tier, with a view to winning promotion back to the Prem.

“London Irish is a huge name in rugby and means a great deal to a lot of people. We want to get the club back where it belongs – on the pitch and competing again,” said Daniels.

“Completing this deal is a major step, but there is plenty of work ahead. We are determined to get the foundations right and build a club that is competitive, sustainable and gives supporters something to believe in. We want London Irish firmly back on the rugby map.”

Jamie Balls, former chair of London Irish Amateur RFC, has been named chief executive, after his search for new investors to revive the pro club led him to Daniels.

Who is Steve Daniels, new London Irish owner?

The 47-year-old built a successful energy business, PE Solutions, which became a partner of the Rugby Football Union and hired former England scrum-half Kyran Bracken as a director.

Daniels played amateur rugby for Colchester and has been heavily involved in Mersey Island RFC, where England head coach Steve Borthwick visited to coach the youth team last year.

Balls said: “Our focus is on creating a resilient, self-sustaining rugby organisation that can stand on its own feet from day one, with the foundations in place to deliver long-term stability, growth and future opportunities.

High cost lender Evlo has tapped bankers for a sale which could fetch the company a valuation of more than £200m, City AM can reveal, in signs of a revival of interest in the controversial subprime lending market.

Evlo, which calls itself ‘the friendly UK lender’ and offers loans at interest rates of up to 252 per cent, has hired advisers at Alantra to run a sale process dubbed ‘Project Oak’, sources told City AM.

The sale could signal a resurgence of investor interest in the sub-prime and high-cost loans market – formerly known as Everyday Loans – which has shrivelled in size since 2019 under scrutiny from regulators and a deluge of claims from borrowers over exploitative lending practices.

Some 250 high-cost credit firms exited the market between 2019 and 2024, while overall lending capacity was down by almost £3bn, according to the Financial Conduct Authority. Sources said investors were now eyeing an opportunity to capitalise on a consumer lending gap, estimated to be around £2bn by consulting group LEK.

Evlo, which operates a network of branches around the country, typically lends to borrowers with minimal credit history or sub-prime credit ratings. Its average customer has an income of around £31,000, according to reports. It reported impairment losses on its loans of £42.2m last year and made a profit of roughly £14.2m.

The company was owned by London-listed Non-Standard Finance before the parent company was hit by thousands of claims from borrowers over allegedly exploitative lending practices.

As part of a scheme of arrangement, in which it set aside some £14m to pay out to customers, Everyday Loans was transferred into a new holding company owned by its lenders. It rebranded as Evlo last year.

Since 2019, a number of the high-cost loan market’s biggest players including Amigo Loans and Wonga.com have gone under after huge compensation claims from borrowers and tighter scrutiny from the Financial Conduct Authority.

Everyday Loans was also reprimanded by the Advertising Standards Authority in 2022 for an advert which suggested that customers could use its loans to pay off their debts with a loan at an interest rate of 99 per cent. 

At the time, Everyday Loans argued it was advertising a “consolidation loan” that could be used to pay off pre-existing debts, which it said was a common financial product offered by numerous regulated lenders. 

“This is a good business that has had some bumps and scrapes,” Evlo boss Jono Gillespie told the Financial Times last year.

Evlo and Alantra declined to comment.

    Sport’s hiking of ticket prices for live sport is completely at odds with many of its marketing efforts and risks alienating future generations of would-be fans, writes Matt Readman.

    Last week, a BBC Sport investigation revealed just how sharply the cost of watching live sport has risen in the UK. Across the Ashes, the Open, Wimbledon, Formula 1, the Ryder Cup and FA Cup, selected ticket prices have increased by an average of around 90 per cent in just a few years – more than twice the rate of inflation.

    Sports executives have rallied to defend this. Operating costs have risen. So too have fan expectations. And, they argue, the profits flow back into grassroots sport. All fair points. But let’s be honest about the underlying reason: they’re raising prices because they can.

    Like any market, ticket prices are governed by supply and demand. And the UK is fortunate that its biggest sporting events have never been more desirable. Sports executives will argue that their prices are justifiably in line with market value. But this is circular logic. 

    Nobody wants to be the one leaving money on the table, but the worry is that live sport’s ticketing market begins to spiral out of control. Keep increasing prices at this rate and we won’t simply change what fans pay, we’ll change what fans we have altogether. 

    There’s a famous line from Jeff Goldblum’s character in Jurassic Park: “Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn’t stop to think if they should.” It’s a question sport needs to ask itself: not whether it can charge these prices, but whether it should.

    We want to get kids off screens but price them out of alternatives

    The first consideration is a moral one. Should sporting institutions take advantage of the very people who sustain them? Fans’ loyalty is valuable. But it also makes them vulnerable.

    The second reflection is political. A recent DCMS report found that adults living in the most deprived parts of the country were only half as likely to attend live sport as those in the least deprived. 

    Sport is part of our national culture. Yet the more expensive it becomes, the more exclusive it gets. If only affluent families can afford to attend major events, we risk cutting entire communities off from the sports that have traditionally brought people together. 

    Sport also needs to be careful it doesn’t sacrifice its long-term commercial health for short-term gains. We know that fandom takes root much earlier than many people realise. Yet ticket prices increasingly prevent young people from experiencing live sport in the way previous generations did.

    There are attempts to address this. The Open, for example, offers free tickets to under-16s. That’s a generous offer in principle, but when an adult ticket costs more than £150 it’s hardly an accessible family day out. And it’s an example that many arenas, where every seat is a valuable commodity, would struggle to follow.

    Meanwhile, a 2026 Youth Sport Trust report found that 77 per cent of parents believe screen use is reducing the time children spend being physically active. We’re desperately trying to get children off screens and into the real world. Yet when it comes to live sport, we’re actively doing the opposite.

    Sport is turning its biggest occasions into playgrounds for the privileged

    Perhaps the biggest frustration for me as a marketer is the contradiction in how these sports brand themselves. 

    Over the past decade I’ve worked on countless briefs, across tennis, golf, cricket and rugby, where the challenge is almost always the same: modernise the brand, become more progressive, more accessible and attract more diverse audiences. In other words, we want to shake off the image that we’re narrow and exclusive.

    But what kind of audience does the Ryder Cup in Ireland expect to attract when tickets cost £430? It won’t be the local kids who might become the next Shane Lowry or Rory McIlroy. It will only reinforce the same stereotypes that sports marketers are being paid to dismantle.

    The irony is that ticket sales often represent only a fraction of the overall revenue generated by major sporting events. Yet in the pursuit of maximising every last pound from a finite number of tickets, we risk turning our biggest sporting occasions into playgrounds for the privileged.

    And that’s the real danger. Not simply that fans are being priced out today, but that the next generation may never feel these places are meant for them in the first place.

    Prima Facie review and star rating: ★★★★

    In London, only 3 per cent of reported rapes lead to a suspect being charged. It is a fact so shocking that even people with no interest in the courts recite it. It is the problem that forms the backdrop of Suzie Miller’s very good 2022 play of the same name as this film, which starred Killing Eve actor Jodie Comer, who in a 100 minutes of theatre astonishingly played every character from the court judge to the victim. 

    Miller’s writing, for which she won the Olivier Award in 2023, extracts a compelling human story out of this institutional crisis. Prima Facie follows Tessa Ensler, a successful criminal defence barrister who has become rich protecting men who are probably guilty of crimes by finding legal loopholes. But an incident in her personal life forces her to rethink the morality of her work. 

    Prima Facie: film can be didactic

    Wicked’s Cynthia Erivo takes over from Comer for Susanna White’s screen adaptation, alongside a supporting cast (Erivo played dozens of characters was presumably harder to land on film). Still, a similar sense of horror is conjured. As Ensler, Erivo brings the sort of muscular fortitude that demonstrates how this young working class woman would graduate to this kind of job that’s typically reserved for the private schooled elite. She is also brilliant at conveying Ensler’s vulnerability; as she experiences a personal breakdown, Erivo’s angular, cocksure barrister softens, her eyes becoming wide chasms of overwhelm.

    There’s an attempt to retain the character-driven intensity of the stage production, via a wealth of tracking shots of Erivo walking past London courthouses and along the river while the camera lingers close. It’s straightforwardly shot and rarely distracted by bells and whistles.

    Harrowing plot

    There have been complaints of didacticness, and at a few points, I am taken briefly out of the action when a line or two is too on-the-nose, moralising about the ways the legal system needs to change. But I’d argue that some of this is inevitable. The story is set in a courtroom, the literal bedrock for conversations about ways to change the world. The one place where you do get to stand up and have your say. Perhaps Prima Facie has an excuse to tell us how to feel more than most. 

    It’s certainly a minor distraction from a terrific depiction of the injustices so many women face, and a truly harrowing plot – multiple women ran out in tears during the London Film Festival screening, and this male critic joined them in weeping throughout. Like the West End show, this Prima Facie finds a compelling and totally shocking human story amid a legal system that seems to have forgotten about the victims. 

    Prima Facie is in UK cinemas on 13 November 2026

    Investing in a football stadium can be the difference between sinking and swimming and the government must play a role, writes Joseph Smith.

    It is fair to say that the Independent Football Regulator’s draft State of the Game report provides the most comprehensive analysis of English football’s finances to date. Published last week and open for consultation until the end of the year, it highlights that while English football is both highly competitive and wealthy it faces significant financial risk.

    The report’s key findings? That 94 per cent of clubs in the top five divisions – from the Premier League down to the National League – operated at a loss, and that two thirds could not survive 90 days without additional funding from existing owners. Nearly 20 EFL and National League clubs reported non-player operating cost figures that were higher than their total revenues.

    The regulator was established because parliament determined that football clubs are not ordinary businesses. Since a club cannot be easily replaced if it fails, the Football Governance Act imposes a level of scrutiny uncommon in most industries.

    The long-standing debate

    Debate has long focused on television revenue – which for the Premier League is into the billions – including redistribution and parachute payments from the top flight. However, the regulator highlights that matchday income becomes increasingly important further down the league pyramid. In the top division it represented 14 per cent of revenue but that rises to 19 per cent in the Championship and 35 per cent in Leagues One and Two.

    Matchday income is therefore essential, and stadium improvements can be a direct way to achieve this. Larger stadiums allow for more ticket sales where demand exists, and enhanced facilities support higher-value matchday and commercial activities – tiers of premium seating have been a popular addition to many stadiums over the last decade. The regulator concludes that investment in stadiums and infrastructure has significantly increased revenue for the largest clubs.

    Premier League clubs benefit from higher ticket prices, stronger demand and corporate hospitality, and invested £2.2bn in infrastructure between 2021/22 and 2024/25. By contrast, League Two clubs invested only £16m. Large clubs can also manage delays and rising costs, while smaller clubs have limited capacity to do so.

    Stadium investment key

    Luton Town is an example of this; the club announced plans to move from Kenilworth Road to Power Court in 2016 but since then the club has moved between divisions while the stadium project faced planning, legal and design hurdles. For smaller clubs such delays could be the difference between spades in the ground and nothing at all.

    The government must therefore step up and reduce some of the planning, transport, land and infrastructure barriers that hinder private investment. The Stadium Regeneration Accelerator announced earlier this year will offer a clear incentive to focus on the largest projects. But the true measure of the initiative is whether government involvement enables projects to go ahead that otherwise would not.

    Stadium investment is part of the solution to a problem that plagues most of the sport. The government should continue supporting major regeneration schemes that create housing, jobs and investment, but the opportunity extends further. The true value of the Stadium Regeneration Accelerator lies in helping viable projects lower down the pyramid overcome barriers that clubs cannot address alone. This would not only support regeneration around football grounds but also help vulnerable clubs build stronger businesses.

    Joseph Smith is a senior consultant at Henham Strategy

    Lewisham’s £1.5bn shopping centre redevelopment freeze, caused by a breakdown between Landsec and the Council, has left residents, traders, and the town centre stranded in uncertainty, says Sergiy Lesyk

    Lewisham shows how a council can lose a £1.5bn scheme and gain nothing.

    Landsec, the property company that has owned Lewisham Shopping Centre for more than 20 years, has put its £1.5bn redevelopment of the centre on hold. Councillors approved the scheme in October 2025, and work had been due to start in 2027. Now nobody can say when, or whether, anything will happen.

    You don’t have to have liked the plans to see the problem that residents and traders in Lewisham now face.

    Landsec gave two reasons: one was the cost of building in London, the other was the Council. In Landsec’s words, recent statements from the Council “make clear that the administration is not able to support the next phase of land assembly needed to unlock delivery without a significant increase in affordable housing.”

    On a social video, the mayor, Liam Shrivastava, had the temerity to state “the conditions for such developments are simply not favourable right now”, and that “the way out of the housing crisis is through building social housing.”

    The mayor was elected on a promise of 1,000 new social rent homes. Instead, the plan to replace the shopping centre with 1,744 homes, including 98 for social rent and 231 at discounted rents or for key workers, will no longer be built. The shopping centre development took about five years to approve, so who really thinks this council will match it any time soon?

    Boots has left its high street unit, which sits in the first phase, for a unit inside the centre. Marks & Spencer, a fixture in Lewisham for almost a century, has closed for good, Natwest has said it will close its branch, and the Model Market food hall still hasn’t reopened.

    Landsec itself says the 1970s building is no longer fit for purpose, as it had been expected to be demolished. 

    Labour, which approved the scheme, and the Greens, who now run the Council, are busy blaming each other, and the mayor is blaming the government. Finger-pointing won’t build a single home or fill a single empty unit.

    Lewisham is being let down

    And the drift goes well beyond the shopping centre. A short walk away, the 649 homes of the Filigree at Lewisham Gateway have stood empty since a flood in February 2025, and residents won’t be back before October 2027. Nearby, one resident told us that food waste bins turned up at their block with no guidance and no collections. The building manager has had to tell everyone not to use them until the council explains what happens next. Even the council’s own website can’t seem to agree on whether flats are getting food waste collections.

    This matters well beyond SE13. London needs homes, and it needs investors with the long-term support and confidence of local councils to build them. 

    So what should happen now?

    First, the council should be straight with residents about what it told Landsec and what it now expects to happen to the site.

    Second, it should publish a support plan for the traders caught up in the uncertainty, because they’re paying for decisions they didn’t make.

    Third, and most importantly, it should set out its own plan for Lewisham town centre. If this scheme wasn’t good enough, the Council needs to show what would be, who will build it, and when.

    Lewisham Conservatives support homes and investment in Lewisham, but not a town centre left in limbo. Residents were promised new homes, a new town centre and a new community. They’ve been let down. The council can’t build any of it until it first rebuilds their trust.

    Sergiy Lesyk is chairman of Lewisham Conservatives

Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:13:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

The first profit, and how thin it was

That changed with the 2025 financial year. According to Bolt’s own results, reported in coverage from Trade with Estonia, the company took €2.27 billion in revenue across more than 50 countries, a 14 percent increase on the year before, and posted its first-ever annual net profit: €920,000. Set against €2.27 billion in revenue, that works out to a margin of roughly four hundredths of one percent, the kind of number that is technically profitable and not much more. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. Villig described the underlying business as having reached a $14 billion gross merchandise value run-rate with two consecutive years of positive cash flow, arguably the more meaningful signal for a company at Bolt’s stage than the net income line itself.

What a four-hundredths-of-a-percent margin actually means

A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. The accounts do not reveal whether Bolt targeted that result or whether it could sustain growth without further external financing. They show a small net profit and positive operating cash flow for the year, not permanent financial independence. It hasn’t settled every question that scale raises, either.

In November 2024, a UK employment tribunal ruled that Bolt’s drivers qualify as workers rather than independent contractors — a ruling on status only, with compensation still to be set at a separate hearing. Leigh Day, the law firm representing roughly 15,000 drivers in the claim, estimates the compensation owed could exceed £200 million, or upwards of £15,000 per driver on average, according to Leigh Day’s own statement. Whether a margin this thin holds, thickens, or gets eaten by exactly that kind of regulatory ruling as Bolt pushes into new cities, verticals and eventually autonomous vehicles is the open question its 2025 results don’t settle either way.

]]> A country of fewer than 1.4 million people has produced ten billion-dollar startups — about 7 for every million residents, more than three times the US rate — and the first of them was a voice-call app a handful of engineers built in Tallinn in 2003. https://siliconcanals.com/n-a-country-of-fewer-than-1-4-million-people-has-produced-ten-billion-dollar-startups-about-7-for-every-million-residents-more-than-three-times-the-us-rate/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 10:00:24 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109711

Estonia ranks second in the cited per-capita tally—and first in the EU—with about 7.1 startups that have reached a billion-dollar valuation per million residents.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: The original excerpt called Estonia the world leader, although the cited per-capita tally places it second behind Liechtenstein. The article also misstated the Tiger Leap school-internet rollout; first-party history says all schools were connected by 2001.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The one that started it

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. Estonian startups collectively reported €3.9 billion in revenue in 2024, up 14.7 percent on the year before, according to Invest in Estonia’s own sector figures, and the sector now employs about 14,400 people directly, or roughly one in every 38 working Estonians, at an average monthly salary of €3,650, more than double the national average. What has held up is the type of company being funded: deep technology, rather than consumer apps or fintech, took 63 percent of all startup investment in 2024, led by rounds for the delivery-robot company Starship Technologies and the green-hydrogen firm Stargate Hydrogen.

A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing.
